119.t: Psalm 119 is an acrostic in Hebrew: it has twenty-two sections of eight verses each, one for each letter of the Hebrew alphabet, and every verse in a section begins with that letter. The KJV prints the letter names (Aleph, Beth, Gimel...) as headings; they are not part of the verse text used here.

Eight words for God's word appear throughout the psalm, nearly one in every verse: law (torah), testimonies (edot), precepts (piqqudim), statutes (chuqqim), commands (mitsvot), laws or judgments (mishpatim), word (davar), and promise (imrah). See 19:7.

136.t: Psalm 136 was sung responsively: a leader sang the first half of each verse and the people answered with the refrain. Jewish tradition calls it the Great Hallel.

"His steadfast love endures forever" (Hebrew ki le'olam chasdo): repeated twenty-six times, once for each verse. The whole of creation and history, from the heavens to daily food, is set within God's covenant faithfulness. See Genesis 24:27 on hesed.

72.t: A prayer for the king: the psalm asks that the king rule with justice and care for the poor, and that his reign be universal and endless. These hopes went beyond any king of Israel and came to be read as a picture of the Messiah's reign. Verse 17 echoes the promise to Abraham (Genesis 12:3).

87.t: Zion, mother of nations: even Israel's enemies, Egypt, Babylon, Philistia, Tyre and Cush, are registered as born in Zion. The psalm looks forward to all nations belonging to God's people (Galatians 4:26).

1:1.t: Psalm titles: the KJV prints a heading above many psalms ("A Psalm of David", "To the chief Musician"). The KJV text used for this translation does not number or include these headings, so they are not translated here. In the Hebrew Bible the heading is usually verse 1, so verse numbers there often run one higher.
"Blessed is the one": the KJV's "Blessed is the man". The Hebrew ish means a man, but the psalm describes anyone who lives this way.

"Blessed" (Hebrew ashre): happy, fortunate, in a right and flourishing condition before God. It is a different word from barukh, "blessed" in the sense of praised or receiving a blessing. Jesus' Beatitudes begin with the Greek equivalent, makarios (Matthew 5:3-11).

1:6.t: "Watches over": the KJV's "knoweth", meaning knows with care and approval.

2:9.t: "Break them": the Greek Old Testament reads "shepherd them", followed in Revelation 2:27 and 19:15.

3:2.t: "Selah": a Hebrew word of uncertain meaning found 71 times in Psalms. It may mark a pause, an instrumental interlude, or a place to lift up the voice. It is left untranslated, as in the KJV.

4:2.t: "Seek false gods": the KJV's "seek after leasing", where "leasing" means lying. The Hebrew may mean lies or false gods.

5:9.t: Paul quotes this verse in Romans 3:13.

6:5.t: "The grave": Hebrew Sheol, the place of the dead, pictured as deep under the earth, where good and bad alike go. In the Old Testament it does not by itself mean a place of punishment. See Genesis 37:35.

6:8.t: Jesus quotes the first line in Matthew 7:23.

7:9.t: "Minds and hearts": the KJV's "hearts and reins", literally "hearts and kidneys", the seat of thought and emotion.

7:12.t: The subject of these verses may be God (as here) or the wicked man preparing weapons that turn back on himself.

8:2.t: Jesus quotes this verse in Matthew 21:16, following the Greek Old Testament: "you have prepared praise".

9:14.t: "Daughter Zion": the KJV's "the daughter of Zion", a poetic name for Jerusalem and its people.

9:16.t: "Higgaion": a musical or meditative term of uncertain meaning, related to hagah, "meditate" (1:2).

9:17.t: "The realm of the dead": the KJV's "hell"; Hebrew Sheol.

10:3.t: "Reviles the LORD": the KJV reads "whom the LORD abhorreth".

11:6.t: "Fiery coals": the KJV's "snares"; a small change in the Hebrew gives "coals".

12:6.t: "Gold refined seven times": the KJV's "a furnace of earth, purified seven times"; the Hebrew is difficult.

12:7.t: "The needy ... us": the KJV reads "keep them ... preserve them", referring to the words of verse 6 or the needy of verse 5.

14:1.t: Paul quotes these verses in Romans 3:10-12 to show that all people are under sin.
"The fool" (Hebrew naval): not someone lacking intelligence, but someone who lives as though God does not matter, a practical atheist who acts as if God does not see or judge. See the note on 10:4.

15:5.t: "Interest": the KJV's "usury", which once meant any interest at all, not only excessive interest. See Exodus 22:25.

16:4.t: "Libations": drink offerings poured out to a god.

16:7.t: "My heart": the KJV's "my reins", the kidneys, seat of the inner life.

16:9.t: "My tongue": the KJV's "my glory". The Greek Old Testament reads "tongue", as quoted in Acts 2:26.

17:4.t: The Hebrew is difficult; the KJV reads "Concerning the works of men, by the word of thy lips I have kept me from the paths of the destroyer."

17:8.t: "Apple of Your eye": the pupil, the most protected part of the eye; see Deuteronomy 32:10.
"The shadow of Your wings": a common picture of God's protection, like a bird sheltering its young (36:7, 57:1, 91:4, Ruth 2:12). Jesus uses it of Jerusalem (Matthew 23:37).

17:14.t: The Hebrew of this verse is difficult and may be read as a curse on the wicked or as a description of their prosperity.

18:2.t: "Horn of my salvation": a horn is a picture of strength, like the horns of a wild ox.

"Rock" (Hebrew sela, tsur): a title for God; a rock is firm, enduring and a place of refuge (see Deuteronomy 32:4). The psalm piles up names for God's protection: rock, fortress, deliverer, shield, horn, stronghold.

18:5.t: "The grave": the KJV's "hell"; Hebrew Sheol. "Confronted": the KJV's "prevented", in the old sense of came before.

18:34.t: "Bronze": the KJV's "steel"; the Hebrew is nechushah, bronze.

18:35.t: "Your help": the KJV's "thy gentleness". The Hebrew anvah means humility or condescension, God stooping down to help.

18:40.t: "Turn their backs in flight": the KJV's "given me the necks of mine enemies".

18:49.t: Paul quotes this verse in Romans 15:9.

19:1.t: "Skies": the KJV's "firmament", the vault of the sky; see Genesis 1:6.

and 19:7-14: the psalm speaks first of God's revelation in creation, which reaches all people without words, then of His revelation in His law, which is "perfect" and restores the soul. Paul draws on both kinds of revelation in Romans 1:20 and 10:18.

19:4.t: "Their voice": the KJV's "their line". The Greek Old Testament reads "their sound", as Paul quotes it in Romans 10:18.

19:12.t: "Hidden faults": the KJV's "secret faults", sins unknown even to the one who commits them.

20:6.t: "Victory": the KJV's "salvation" or "saving strength". The Hebrew yeshuah means rescue or deliverance from real danger, often victory in battle; see Exodus 14:13.

21:1.t: "Victory": the KJV's "salvation" or "saving strength". The Hebrew yeshuah means rescue or deliverance from real danger, often victory in battle; see Exodus 14:13.

21:3.t: "Came to greet him": the KJV's "preventest him", in the old sense of going before.

21:8.t: These verses address the king, so "your" is lowercase; verses 1-7 and 13 address the LORD.

22:3.t: The Hebrew may be read "enthroned on the praises of Israel" (KJV "inhabitest the praises").

22:12.t: Bashan: a fertile region east of the Jordan known for strong cattle.

22:15.t: "My mouth": the KJV's "my strength"; a small change in the Hebrew gives "my palate".

22:20.t: "My precious life": the KJV's "my darling", literally "my only one", meaning his one life.

22:21.t: "Wild oxen": the KJV's "unicorns". "Save me": the KJV reads "thou hast heard me". The Hebrew anitani means "You have answered me", the turning point of the psalm from lament to praise.

22:29.t: "The rich": the KJV's "they that be fat".

24:4.t: "Trust in an idol or swear by a false god": the KJV's "lifted up his soul unto vanity, nor sworn deceitfully".

24:6.t: "O God of Jacob": the KJV reads "O Jacob". The Greek and Syriac add "God of".

25:14.t: "Confides in": the KJV's "the secret of the LORD is with". The Hebrew sod means a circle of close friends or confidential counsel; see Job 29:4.

26:2.t: "Heart and mind": the KJV's "reins and heart".

26:6.t: "Wash my hands in innocence": a sign of being free from guilt; compare Deuteronomy 21:6.

27:13.t: "I would have lost heart": the KJV supplies "I had fainted". The Hebrew begins with an unfinished "Unless..."

28:2.t: "Most Holy Place": the KJV's "holy oracle", the inner room of the sanctuary where God spoke.

28:8.t: "His people": the KJV reads "their strength"; a small change in the Hebrew gives "His people".

29:1.t: "Heavenly beings": the KJV's "O ye mighty". The Hebrew bene elim, "sons of gods", means the angels, the heavenly beings who serve in God's court, as in Job 1:6.

29:2.t: "In the splendor of His holiness": the KJV's "in the beauty of holiness". The Hebrew may also mean "in holy attire".

29:6.t: Sirion: the Sidonian name for Mount Hermon; see Deuteronomy 3:9. "Wild ox": the KJV's "unicorn".

29:9.t: "Makes the deer give birth": the KJV's "maketh the hinds to calve". A different reading gives "twists the oaks".

30:7.t: "My royal mountain": the KJV's "my mountain". The Hebrew is literally "my mountain", perhaps Zion as the seat of David's kingdom.

30:12.t: "My heart": the KJV's "my glory"; the Hebrew kavod sometimes means the inner self.

31:21.t: "In a city under siege": the KJV's "in a strong city".

31:23.t: "Pays back in full": the KJV's "plentifully rewardeth the proud doer", meaning repays them as they deserve.

32:4.t: "My strength was sapped": the KJV's "my moisture is turned into the drought of summer".

33:2.t: "Lyre ... ten-stringed harp": the KJV's "harp ... psaltery and an instrument of ten strings".

33:7.t: "Into jars": the KJV's "as an heap". The Hebrew ned can mean a heap or, with different vowels, a jar or wineskin.

34:10.t: "The lions": the KJV's "the young lions". The Greek Old Testament reads "the rich".

34:12.t: Peter quotes these verses in 1 Peter 3:10-12.

35:3.t: "Javelin": the KJV's "stop the way". The Hebrew segor may name a weapon.
"I am your salvation" (Hebrew yeshu'atekh ani): yeshuah, salvation or deliverance, rescue from real danger; see Exodus 14:13.

35:13.t: "When my prayers returned to me unanswered": the KJV's "my prayer returned into mine own bosom". The phrase may also mean he prayed with head bowed on his chest.

35:15.t: "Assailants": the KJV's "the abjects", meaning outcasts or smiters.

35:19.t: Jesus applies "hate me without reason" to Himself in John 15:25 (see also 69:4).

36:1.t: The KJV reads "The transgression of the wicked saith within my heart". The Hebrew begins with ne'um, an oracle: "Transgression speaks to the wicked deep in his heart." Paul quotes the second half in Romans 3:18.

37:3.t: "Enjoy safe pasture": the KJV's "verily thou shalt be fed". The Hebrew may also mean "cultivate faithfulness".

37:9.t: "Inherit the land": the KJV's "inherit the earth" in verses 9, 11 and 22. The Hebrew erets means both. Jesus quotes verse 11 in Matthew 5:5: "the meek ... shall inherit the earth."

37:11.t: "Inherit the land": the KJV's "inherit the earth" in verses 9, 11 and 22. The Hebrew erets means both. Jesus quotes verse 11 in Matthew 5:5: "the meek ... shall inherit the earth."
"The meek" (Hebrew anavim): the humble, the lowly, those who depend on God rather than seizing power. See Numbers 12:3 on Moses.

37:22.t: "Inherit the land": the KJV's "inherit the earth" in verses 9, 11 and 22. The Hebrew erets means both. Jesus quotes verse 11 in Matthew 5:5: "the meek ... shall inherit the earth."

37:29.t: "Inherit the land": the KJV's "inherit the earth" in verses 9, 11 and 22. The Hebrew erets means both. Jesus quotes verse 11 in Matthew 5:5: "the meek ... shall inherit the earth."

37:34.t: "Inherit the land": the KJV's "inherit the earth" in verses 9, 11 and 22. The Hebrew erets means both. Jesus quotes verse 11 in Matthew 5:5: "the meek ... shall inherit the earth."

37:20.t: "The beauty of the fields": the KJV's "the fat of lambs". The Hebrew kar can mean pasture or lamb.

37:35.t: "A luxuriant native tree": the KJV's "a green bay tree".

37:37.t: "A future awaits those who seek peace": the KJV's "the end of that man is peace". The Hebrew acharit means future or posterity.

38:11.t: "Friends and companions": the KJV's "my lovers and my friends".

39:5.t: "Handbreadth": about 7.5 centimeters, a picture of shortness.
"Breath" (Hebrew hevel): a vapor or breath, something fleeting and insubstantial. The KJV's "vanity". It is the key word of Ecclesiastes ("Meaningless! Meaningless!").

39:13.t: "Look away from me": the KJV's "O spare me". The Hebrew asks God to turn His gaze of judgment away.

40:6.t: "My ears You have opened": the KJV's "mine ears hast thou opened", literally "ears You have dug for me". The Greek Old Testament reads "a body You have prepared for me", the form quoted in Hebrews 10:5.

"Sacrifice and offering You did not desire ... I delight to do Your will": God values obedience above ritual (1 Samuel 15:22). Hebrews 10:5-10 places these words in Christ's mouth as He comes into the world, offering His own body in obedience once for all.

40:13.t: These verses are nearly identical to Psalm 70.

41:9.t: "Has turned against me": the KJV's "hath lifted up his heel against me". Jesus quotes this verse of Judas (John 13:18).

41:13.t: This doxology closes Book One of the Psalms (Psalms 1-41). The Psalms are divided into five books, each ending with a blessing: 41:13, 72:19, 89:52, 106:48 and 150.

42:4.t: "Under the protection of the Mighty One": the KJV's "with the multitude". The Hebrew is uncertain.

42:6.t: Mizar: a small peak near Mount Hermon, at the headwaters of the Jordan, far from Jerusalem.

42:11.t: "My Savior": the KJV's "the health of my countenance", literally "the salvation of my face".

43:5.t: "My Savior": the KJV's "the health of my countenance", literally "the salvation of my face".

44:19.t: "A haunt for jackals": the KJV's "the place of dragons". "Deep darkness": the KJV's "the shadow of death".

44:22.t: Paul quotes this verse in Romans 8:36.

45:1.t: "Recite my verses": the KJV's "I speak of the things which I have made".

45:4.t: "Let Your right hand achieve awesome deeds": the KJV's "thy right hand shall teach thee terrible things".

45:8.t: "The music of the strings": the KJV's "whereby they have made thee glad". The Hebrew minni may mean "stringed instruments".

45:12.t: "The city of Tyre": the KJV's "the daughter of Tyre".

45:13.t: "Within her chamber": the KJV's "all glorious within", meaning inside the palace.

47:9.t: "Kings": the KJV's "shields", a poetic term for rulers who protect their people.

48:2.t: "Like the heights of the north": the KJV's "on the sides of the north". The Hebrew tsaphon is also the name of a mountain the Canaanites believed was the home of their gods; Zion is the true holy mountain.

48:7.t: Ships of Tarshish: large ocean-going ships, named for a distant port, probably in Spain.

48:11.t: "Villages of Judah": the KJV's "daughters of Judah".

48:14.t: "Even to the end": the KJV's "even unto death". The Hebrew al-muth may be a musical term carried over from a heading.

49:5.t: "Wicked deceivers": the KJV's "the iniquity of my heels".

49:11.t: "Their tombs": the KJV's "their inward thought". The Greek and Syriac read qivram, "their graves", for qirbam.

49:14.t: "Grave": Hebrew Sheol, here and in verse 15.

50:1.t: "The Mighty One, God, the LORD": the Hebrew el elohim YHWH, three names of God together.

51:5.t: The verse describes the psalmist's sinfulness from the very beginning of life; it does not say that conception or birth is sinful.

51:6.t: "Even in the womb ... in that secret place": the KJV's "in the inward parts ... in the hidden part".

51:14.t: "The guilt of bloodshed": the KJV's "bloodguiltiness". The traditional heading connects this psalm to David's sin with Bathsheba and the murder of Uriah (2 Samuel 11-12).

52:1.t: "Mighty man": the KJV's "O mighty man", spoken with irony to a powerful evildoer. Some modern Bibles read the second line as "you who are a disgrace in God's eyes"; the KJV reading is kept.

55:15.t: "The realm of the dead": the KJV's "hell"; Hebrew Sheol. "Alive": the KJV's "quick".

55:19.t: "Who does not change": the KJV reads "Because they have no changes", referring to the wicked. The Hebrew allows both.

56:8.t: "Bottle": a leather flask. The picture is of God collecting every tear.

57:4.t: "Ravenous beasts": the KJV's "them that are set on fire".

57:7.t: These verses appear again in Psalm 108:1-5.

57:8.t: "My soul": the KJV's "my glory"; the Hebrew kavod sometimes means the inner self (see 30:12). "I will awaken the dawn": the KJV's "I myself will awake early".

58:1.t: "You rulers": the KJV's "O congregation". The Hebrew elem may mean "silence" or, with different vowels, "gods", meaning rulers or judges.

58:9.t: The Hebrew is obscure; the KJV reads "both living, and in his wrath".

58:10.t: The language is the strong imagery of victory in ancient warfare; it expresses longing for God's justice, not personal revenge.

59:9.t: "You are my strength, I watch for You": the KJV reads "Because of his strength will I wait upon thee". A few Hebrew manuscripts read "my strength", matching verse 17.

59:10.t: "Will go before me": the KJV's "shall prevent me", in the old sense.

60:4.t: "Against the bow": the KJV reads "because of the truth". The Hebrew qoshet can mean "truth" or, spelled differently, "bow".

60:5.t: These verses appear again in Psalm 108:6-13.

60:8.t: "Washbasin ... toss My sandal": pictures of Moab and Edom as servants; throwing a sandal over land may signify claiming ownership (compare Ruth 4:7).

62:1.t: "Finds rest": the KJV's "waiteth". The Hebrew dumiyyah means silence, quiet trust.

62:5.t: "Finds rest": the KJV's "waiteth". The Hebrew dumiyyah means silence, quiet trust.

62:9.t: "Breath": the KJV's "vanity"; Hebrew hevel, a vapor or breath, something fleeting and insubstantial. See 39:5.

62:12.t: Paul echoes the last line in Romans 2:6.

65:1.t: "Awaits": the KJV's "waiteth". The Greek reads "is fitting". "Zion": the KJV spells it Sion here.

65:3.t: "You forgave": the KJV's "thou shalt purge them away"; the Hebrew kipper is "atone for", to remove guilt and defilement so that the relationship with God is restored; see Exodus 29:33.

65:11.t: "Your carts": the KJV's "thy paths", the tracks of God's chariot across the land.

67:1.t: This verse echoes the priestly blessing of Numbers 6:24-25.

68:1.t: These words echo Moses' cry when the ark set out (Numbers 10:35).

68:4.t: "Rides on the heavens": the KJV's "rideth upon the heavens". Some read "rides through the deserts".

"Yah" (Hebrew YH): a short form of the divine name YHWH, God's personal name, probably pronounced Yahweh, which the KJV usually prints LORD. Here the KJV prints JAH. It appears in "Hallelujah", "praise Yah". See Genesis 2:4 and Exodus 6:3.

68:6.t: "With singing": the KJV's "bound with chains". The Hebrew kosharot is uncertain.

68:11.t: "The women who proclaim it": the Hebrew word is feminine, as in the KJV margin. The KJV text reads "those that published it".

68:13.t: The Hebrew of this verse is obscure; the KJV reads "Though ye have lien among the pots".

68:14.t: Zalmon: a mountain near Shechem. The KJV spells it Salmon.

68:15.t: "Majestic ... rugged mountain": the KJV reads "The hill of God is as the hill of Bashan". The Hebrew compares the high peaks of Bashan with lowly Zion, which God chose.

68:17.t: "Has come from Sinai into His sanctuary": the KJV reads "the Lord is among them, as in Sinai, in the holy place".

68:19.t: "Bears our burdens": the KJV's "loadeth us with benefits". The Hebrew can mean either "carries us" or "bears our load".

68:26.t: "In the assembly of Israel": the KJV's "from the fountain of Israel".

68:30.t: "The beast among the reeds": the KJV's "the company of spearmen", probably Egypt pictured as a crocodile or hippopotamus.

69:1.t: "Up to my neck": the KJV's "come in unto my soul"; nephesh here means throat or neck.

69:22.t: Paul quotes these verses in Romans 11:9-10.

69:25.t: Peter applies this verse to Judas in Acts 1:20.

69:28.t: "The book of life": the KJV's "the book of the living", God's record of His people. See Exodus 32:32.

72:10.t: "Distant shores": the KJV's "the isles", the coastlands of the Mediterranean.

72:19.t: This doxology closes Book Two of the Psalms (Psalms 42-72).

72:20.t: This note was probably placed at the end of an early collection of David's psalms; other psalms of David appear later in the book.

73:4.t: "They have no struggles": the KJV's "there are no bands in their death".

73:7.t: "From their callous hearts comes iniquity": the KJV's "Their eyes stand out with fatness". The Greek and Syriac support "iniquity".

73:10.t: The Hebrew of this verse is obscure.

74:4.t: "The place where You met with us": the KJV's "thy congregations".

74:8.t: "Every place where God was worshiped": the KJV's "all the synagogues of God", meeting places, not the later synagogues.

74:13.t: "The monster": the KJV's "the dragons"; Hebrew tannin, a sea monster. See Job 7:12.

75:6.t: "From the desert": the KJV's "from the south". The Hebrew midbar harim may also be read "the desert of the mountains".

76:2.t: Salem: an old name for Jerusalem (Genesis 14:18).

76:4.t: "Rich with game": the KJV's "the mountains of prey".

77:2.t: "I stretched out untiring hands": the KJV's "my sore ran in the night". The Hebrew yad, "hand", is read "sore" in the KJV.

77:10.t: "To this I will appeal": the KJV reads "This is my infirmity". The Hebrew is difficult.

77:13.t: "Holy": the KJV's "in the sanctuary"; the Hebrew baqqodesh can mean either.

78:2.t: Matthew 13:35 quotes this verse of Jesus' teaching in parables.
"Parable" (Hebrew mashal): a saying, proverb or story that teaches. "Hidden things" (chidot): riddles, things whose meaning must be drawn out. The psalm retells Israel's history as a lesson.

78:12.t: Zoan: a city in the Nile delta, also called Tanis.

78:43.t: Zoan: a city in the Nile delta, also called Tanis.

78:24.t: "Grain of heaven": the KJV's "the corn of heaven", the manna. Jesus refers to this in John 6:31-33.

78:47.t: "Sycamore figs": the KJV's "sycomore trees", a fig tree, not the North American sycamore.

78:51.t: "The tents of Ham": Egypt, descended from Ham (Genesis 10:6).

78:60.t: Shiloh: the place where the tabernacle stood in the time of the judges (1 Samuel 1-4). Its destruction is recalled in Jeremiah 7:12.

78:61.t: "The ark of His might": the KJV's "his strength", the ark of the covenant, captured by the Philistines (1 Samuel 4).

79:12.t: "Into the laps": the KJV's "into their bosom", the fold of a garment used as a pocket.

80:1.t: "Between the cherubim": the cherubim are winged heavenly beings who guard God's holiness and surround His throne; two golden cherubim stood over the ark. See Exodus 25:18-22.

80:11.t: "The Sea ... the River": the Mediterranean and the Euphrates, the ideal borders of the land.

80:15.t: "The son": the KJV's "the branch". The Hebrew ben means son; the vine and the son both picture Israel.

81:3.t: "Ram's horn": the KJV's "trumpet"; Hebrew shofar. "When the moon is full": the KJV's "in the time appointed".

81:5.t: "A voice we had not known": the KJV's "a language that I understood not".

81:6.t: "Basket": the KJV's "pots", the baskets used to carry clay for bricks in Egypt.

83:6.t: Hagrites: the KJV's "Hagarenes", an Arabian tribe.

83:9.t: These recall Gideon's and Deborah's victories (Judges 4-8).

83:13.t: "Tumbleweed": the KJV's "a wheel", a whirling plant blown by the wind.

84:5.t: "Whose hearts are set on pilgrimage": the KJV's "in whose heart are the ways of them", literally "highways in their heart", the roads to Jerusalem.

84:6.t: "Valley of Baca": a dry valley; baca may mean "weeping" or a kind of balsam tree.

85:1.t: "Restored the fortunes": the KJV's "brought back the captivity". The Hebrew phrase shuv shevut can mean either. See Deuteronomy 30:3.

86:2.t: "Faithful": the KJV's "holy"; Hebrew chasid, one who is devoted, a word related to hesed, loyal love. See 16:10.

86:13.t: "The grave": the KJV's "the lowest hell"; Hebrew Sheol.

86:16.t: "Just as my mother did": the KJV's "the son of thine handmaid", a servant born into the household.

87:4.t: "Rahab": here a poetic name for Egypt (Isaiah 30:7), not the sea monster. Cush: the KJV's "Ethiopia".

88:5.t: "Set apart": the KJV's "free". "From Your care": the KJV's "from thy hand".

88:11.t: "Destruction": the KJV's "destruction"; Hebrew Abaddon, a name for the realm of the dead.

88:18.t: "Darkness is my closest friend": the KJV reads "and mine acquaintance into darkness". The Hebrew allows both.

89:6.t: "Heavenly beings": the KJV's "sons of the mighty"; the Hebrew bene elim, "sons of gods", means the angels (see 29:1).

89:10.t: Rahab: a mythical sea monster, a picture of chaos, unrelated to Rahab of Jericho; see Job 9:13.

89:12.t: Tabor and Hermon: two prominent mountains in northern Israel.

89:15.t: "Learned to acclaim You": the KJV's "know the joyful sound", the festival shout.

89:18.t: The KJV text reads "the LORD is our defence; and the Holy One of Israel is our king", with the reading used here in its margin.

89:19.t: "Your faithful people": the KJV's "thy holy one". Some Hebrew manuscripts read the plural.

89:52.t: This doxology closes Book Three of the Psalms (Psalms 73-89).

90:5.t: "Sweep people away in the sleep of death": the KJV's "carriest them away as with a flood; they are as a sleep".

90:9.t: "With a sigh": the KJV's "as a tale that is told".

90:13.t: "Relent": the KJV's "let it repent thee"; Hebrew nacham, to be sorry, grieved or moved to change course. See Genesis 6:6.

93:3.t: "Seas": the KJV's "floods". The roaring waters picture the forces of chaos that the LORD rules over.

94:11.t: Paul quotes this verse in 1 Corinthians 3:20.

94:17.t: "The silence of death": the KJV's "silence", the grave.

95:8.t: "Meribah ... Massah": the KJV's "the provocation ... the day of temptation", which translate these place names: Meribah means "quarreling" and Massah "testing". See Exodus 17:7.

96:13.t: "Let all creation rejoice": supplied for clarity; the KJV continues the sentence from verse 12, "then shall all the trees of the wood rejoice before the LORD".

97:1.t: "The LORD reigns" (Hebrew YHWH malakh): the theme of Psalms 93-99, celebrating God as King over creation and all nations.

97:7.t: The Greek Old Testament reads "worship Him, all you His angels", quoted in Hebrews 1:6 (see also Deuteronomy 32:43).

97:11.t: "Light shines": the KJV's "Light is sown". A small change in the Hebrew gives "dawns".

99:1.t: "Between the cherubim": the cherubim are winged heavenly beings who guard God's holiness and surround His throne; two golden cherubim stood over the ark. See Exodus 25:18-22.

99:4.t: "The King is mighty, He loves justice": the KJV reads "The king's strength also loveth judgment".

99:5.t: "His footstool": the ark of the covenant, or the temple, pictured as the footstool of God's throne (1 Chronicles 28:2).

100:3.t: "And we are His": the KJV follows the Hebrew written text, "and not we ourselves". The scribes' marginal reading, lo, "His", is followed here; the two words sound the same in Hebrew.

101:8.t: "Every morning": the morning was the usual time for a king to hear cases.

102:6.t: "Desert owl": the KJV's "pelican of the wilderness". The Hebrew bird name is uncertain.

103:5.t: "Like the eagle's": the eagle, which renews its feathers each year, pictures restored strength (Isaiah 40:31).

103:20.t: "Mighty ones": the KJV's "that excel in strength".

104:4.t: "He makes the winds His messengers": the KJV's "Who maketh his angels spirits". The Hebrew malakh means messenger or angel, and ruach means wind or spirit, so both readings are possible. Hebrews 1:7 quotes the verse in the KJV's sense.

104:35.t: "Praise the LORD": the Hebrew is hallelu-yah, the first time this phrase appears in the Psalms.

105:15.t: "My anointed ones": here the patriarchs, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.

105:18.t: "His neck was put in irons": the KJV's "he was laid in iron", literally "his soul came into iron".

105:22.t: "To instruct": the KJV's "to bind"; the Greek and Syriac read "to teach".

105:28.t: "For had they not rebelled": the KJV reads "and they rebelled not against his word", meaning Moses and Aaron obeyed. The Hebrew allows both.

105:31.t: "Gnats": the KJV's "lice". The Hebrew word may mean gnats, lice or mosquitoes. See Exodus 8:16.

106:15.t: "A wasting disease": the KJV's "leanness into their soul". See Numbers 11:33.

106:28.t: "Lifeless gods": the KJV's "the dead", idols that have no life. At Peor Israel joined the Moabites in worshiping Baal (see Numbers 25).

106:33.t: "The Spirit of God": the KJV's "his spirit", which may refer to God's Spirit (Isaiah 63:10) or to Moses' spirit.

106:48.t: This doxology closes Book Four of the Psalms (Psalms 90-106).

107:10.t: "The deepest gloom": the KJV's "the shadow of death"; see 23:4.

107:14.t: "The deepest gloom": the KJV's "the shadow of death"; see 23:4.

107:29.t: Jesus' stilling of the storm (Mark 4:39-41) echoes this verse.

109:6.t: "An accuser": the KJV's "Satan"; Hebrew satan, an adversary, here an accuser in court. In Job the same word, with the article, names the heavenly accuser (see Job 1:6).

The curses: this is the strongest of the cursing psalms. The psalmist hands vengeance over to God instead of taking it himself (compare Deuteronomy 32:35). Jesus taught His followers to bless those who curse them (Luke 6:28), and Paul says the same (Romans 12:14).

109:8.t: Peter applies this verse to Judas in Acts 1:20.

110:3.t: The Hebrew of this verse is very difficult, and translations vary widely.

110:7.t: "He will drink from a brook along the way": a picture of the victorious king refreshed in pursuit of his enemies.

112:9.t: Paul quotes this verse in 2 Corinthians 9:9.

113:7.t: "Ash heap": the KJV's "dunghill", the town rubbish heap where beggars sat.

116:10.t: "I trusted ... when I said": the KJV's "I believed, therefore have I spoken", the Greek reading that Paul quotes in 2 Corinthians 4:13.

116:16.t: "I serve You just as my mother did": the KJV's "the son of thine handmaid", a servant born into the household; see 86:16.

118:27.t: "With boughs in hand, join in the festal procession": the KJV's "bind the sacrifice with cords, even unto the horns of the altar". The Hebrew chag may mean a festival or the festal sacrifice.

119:83.t: "A wineskin in the smoke": a leather bottle hung near the fire, dried out and shriveled.

119:96.t: "To all perfection I see a limit": everything in creation has an end, but God's word has none.

119:113.t: "Double-minded people": the KJV's "vain thoughts". The Hebrew se'aphim means divided or wavering people.

119:147.t: "I rise before dawn ... my eyes stay open": the KJV's "I prevented the dawning of the morning ... Mine eyes prevent the night watches", in the old sense of "come before".

120:4.t: "Broom bush": the KJV's "juniper", whose wood burns hot and long.

120:5.t: Meshech and Kedar: distant, hostile peoples, in the far north and the Arabian desert, a picture of living among enemies.

121:1.t: "I lift up my eyes to the mountains; where does my help come from?": the KJV punctuation reads it as a statement. The Hebrew is best taken as a question, answered in verse 2.

125:3.t: "Scepter": the KJV's "rod", a symbol of ruling power.

126:1.t: "Restored the fortunes": the KJV's "turned again the captivity". The Hebrew phrase shuv shevut can mean either. See Deuteronomy 30:3.

126:4.t: "Restored the fortunes": the KJV's "turned again the captivity". The Hebrew phrase shuv shevut can mean either. See Deuteronomy 30:3.
"Streams in the Negev": the KJV's "streams in the south", dry riverbeds in the southern desert that suddenly fill with water after rain.

127:5.t: "In court": the KJV's "in the gate", where legal cases were heard.

129:6.t: "Grass on the roof": grass sprouting in the thin soil of flat roofs, which withers quickly.

131:2.t: "A weaned child": a child no longer crying to be fed, content simply to be with its mother; a picture of quiet trust.

132:6.t: "The fields of Jaar": the KJV's "the fields of the wood". Jaar is probably Kiriath Jearim, where the ark stayed before David brought it to Jerusalem (1 Samuel 7:1-2, 2 Samuel 6).

132:8.t: These verses appear in Solomon's prayer at the temple dedication (2 Chronicles 6:41-42).

132:11.t: Peter cites this promise in Acts 2:30.

133:2.t: "Collar": the KJV's "skirts", the edge or opening of the robe.

133:3.t: Mount Hermon, in the far north, was known for heavy dew; the picture is of rich blessing falling on Zion.

137:7.t: "On the day Jerusalem fell": the Babylonian destruction of 586 BC, when Edom cheered and joined in (Obadiah 10-14).

137:9.t: The verse is a cry of anguish from exiles who had seen their own children killed (2 Kings 25, Lamentations 2:20). It asks for the justice the prophets had announced against Babylon (Isaiah 13:16), leaving vengeance with God rather than prescribing conduct.

138:2.t: "You have exalted Your word above all Your name": the Hebrew is difficult; it may mean God's promise has surpassed all that His name was known for.

139:15.t: "In the depths of the earth": a poetic picture of the hidden place of the womb.

141:5.t: The Hebrew of these verses is very obscure, and translations differ widely.

143:2.t: Paul draws on this verse in Romans 3:20 and Galatians 2:16.

144:2.t: "My loving God": the KJV's "My goodness"; Hebrew chasdi, "my steadfast love".

144:3.t: Compare 8:4, "What is man ... the son of man", where both phrases mean a human being.

144:12.t: The Hebrew of these verses is difficult in places.

148:7.t: "Great sea creatures": the KJV's "dragons"; Hebrew tanninim, a word that covers any large sea animal, as in Genesis 1:21.

150:3.t: "Lyre", "pipe": the KJV's "psaltery" and "organs". The "organ" was a simple wind instrument such as a flute.

1:2.t: "Law" (Hebrew torah): instruction or teaching, not only commands. In Psalms it means God's whole revealed word. "Meditates" (hagah) means to murmur or mutter, reading aloud to oneself and pondering.

2:2.t: "His Anointed ... My Son": the psalm was first sung of David's line of kings, whom God called His sons (2 Samuel 7:14). The New Testament applies it to Jesus the Messiah (Acts 4:25-27, 13:33, Hebrews 1:5, 5:5). "Anointed" is mashiach, one marked out with oil for an office, the word that gives us Messiah; see Leviticus 4:3. Following the KJV, which capitalizes "Son", the pronouns for the Anointed are capitalized in this psalm.

2:7.t: "His Anointed ... My Son": the psalm was first sung of David's line of kings, whom God called His sons (2 Samuel 7:14). The New Testament applies it to Jesus the Messiah (Acts 4:25-27, 13:33, Hebrews 1:5, 5:5). "Anointed" is mashiach, one marked out with oil for an office, the word that gives us Messiah; see Leviticus 4:3. Following the KJV, which capitalizes "Son", the pronouns for the Anointed are capitalized in this psalm.

"Today I have become Your Father": the KJV's "this day have I begotten thee". The phrase describes the king's enthronement as adoption by God. The New Testament applies it to Jesus' resurrection and exaltation (Acts 13:33).

2:12.t: "His Anointed ... My Son": the psalm was first sung of David's line of kings, whom God called His sons (2 Samuel 7:14). The New Testament applies it to Jesus the Messiah (Acts 4:25-27, 13:33, Hebrews 1:5, 5:5). "Anointed" is mashiach, one marked out with oil for an office, the word that gives us Messiah; see Leviticus 4:3. Following the KJV, which capitalizes "Son", the pronouns for the Anointed are capitalized in this psalm.

"Kiss the Son" (Hebrew nashsheqo bar): bar is the Aramaic word for "son". Kissing was a sign of homage to a king. Some read the Hebrew differently ("kiss purely" or "kiss His feet"); the KJV reading is kept.
"Take refuge" (Hebrew chasah): to seek shelter, as under a rock or a bird's wings. The KJV's "put their trust in" captures the meaning; refuge is one of the most common pictures of faith in Psalms.

5:11.t: "Take refuge" (Hebrew chasah): to seek shelter, as under a rock or a bird's wings. The KJV's "put their trust in" captures the meaning; refuge is one of the most common pictures of faith in Psalms.

5:7.t: "Steadfast love" (Hebrew hesed): the KJV's "mercy". hesed is loyal, committed love that keeps its promises, especially within a covenant; no single English word covers it, and the KJV uses "mercy", "kindness" and "lovingkindness". See Genesis 24:27. This word appears over 120 times in Psalms.

6:4.t: "Steadfast love" (Hebrew hesed): the KJV's "mercies". hesed is loyal, committed love that keeps its promises, especially within a covenant; no single English word covers it, and the KJV uses "mercy", "kindness" and "lovingkindness". See Genesis 24:27.

8:4.t: "What is man ... the son of man" (Hebrew enosh ... ben adam): both mean a human being. Job parodies this verse (Job 7:17). Hebrews 2:6-9 applies verses 4-6 to Jesus, who as a true man was made lower than the angels for a little while and is now crowned with glory.

8:5.t: "Than the angels" (Hebrew me'elohim): elohim usually means "God", and the verse can be read "a little lower than God", as many modern Bibles do. The KJV follows the Greek Old Testament, "angels", which Hebrews 2:7 quotes.

8:6.t: "Under his feet": Paul applies this to Christ's rule over all things (1 Corinthians 15:27, Ephesians 1:22).

10:4.t: "There is no room for God" (Hebrew en elohim): literally "there is no God". The wicked man is a practical atheist: he lives as if God does not see or judge. Compare 14:1.

16:5.t: "Portion ... cup ... lot": the LORD Himself is the psalmist's inheritance, as He was for the Levites, who received no land (Numbers 18:20).

16:10.t: "The realm of the dead ... Your Holy One ... decay" (Hebrew she'ol; chasidekha; shachat): Peter (Acts 2:25-31) and Paul (Acts 13:35-37) quote this verse from the Greek Old Testament, arguing that David died and his body decayed, so the promise points to the Messiah's resurrection. Chasid, "faithful one" or "holy one", is related to hesed; the KJV capitalizes it, following this reading.

16:11.t: "The path of life": both the way to live and the way to life itself, a life that continues in God's presence.

17:15.t: "When I awake": the psalmist's hope of seeing God's face goes beyond the night of danger; many readers find in it a hope beyond death.

18:1.t: "I love You" (Hebrew erchamkha): a rare form of racham, the word for tender, motherly love, from rechem, "womb" (see Exodus 34:6, "compassionate"). It is unusual for a person to use this word of love for God.

18:25.t: "To the faithful You show Yourself faithful": God's dealings correspond to each person's character. "Faithful" (chasid) is related to hesed. "Shrewd" means God outwits the crooked; He is never Himself crooked.

19:7.t: "Law ... testimony ... precepts ... commands ... fear ... decrees": six names for God's word, each with a different shade: torah (instruction), edut (witness), piqqudim (charges), mitsvah (command), yir'ah (reverence), mishpatim (rulings). Psalm 119 develops the same vocabulary.

19:13.t: "Willful sins" (Hebrew zedim, "presumptuous things"): sins done in arrogance, in contrast to hidden faults (verse 12). The law treats sin "with a high hand", open defiance of God, as far more serious than unintentional sin (see Numbers 15:30).

19:14.t: "My Redeemer" (Hebrew go'ali): from ga'al, to buy back or rescue as a family member. The go'el was the family member who bought back land, freed a kinsman from slavery, or avenged his blood; God acts as His people's next of kin. See Exodus 6:6 and Job 19:25.

22:1.t: "My God, my God, why have You forsaken me?": Jesus cried these words from the cross (Matthew 27:46, Mark 15:34), in Aramaic. By quoting the first line, He claimed the whole psalm, which moves from abandonment to worldwide praise. The Gospels show its details fulfilled in His death: mocking and shaking heads (22:7-8, Matthew 27:39-43), thirst (22:15, John 19:28), and dividing His clothes (22:18, John 19:23-24).

22:16.t: "They pierce my hands and my feet" (Hebrew ka'aru, as the Greek Old Testament and the KJV read it): the standard Hebrew text reads ka'ari, "like a lion my hands and my feet". The difference is one small letter. Some Dead Sea Scroll evidence supports the reading "dig" or "pierce". The KJV reading is kept, following the Greek, Syriac and Latin translations.

22:22.t: "I will declare Your name to my brothers": Hebrews 2:12 places these words in the mouth of Christ, who is not ashamed to call His people brothers.

22:31.t: "He has done it!" (Hebrew ki asah): compare Jesus' final word, "It is finished" (John 19:30).

23:3.t: "Soul" (Hebrew nephesh): a living, breathing creature, a whole person, not a soul separate from the body; here it means the whole person, life itself (see Genesis 2:7). "He restores my soul" means He brings me back to life and strength.

23:6.t: "Steadfast love" (Hebrew hesed): the KJV's "mercy". hesed is loyal, committed love that keeps its promises, especially within a covenant; no single English word covers it, and the KJV uses "mercy", "kindness" and "lovingkindness" (see Genesis 24:27). "Follow" (radaph) is a strong word, usually "pursue" or "chase": God's goodness and love run after the psalmist.

24:1.t: "The earth is the LORD's": Paul quotes this in 1 Corinthians 10:26.

24:10.t: "The LORD of hosts" (Hebrew YHWH tseva'ot): hosts are armies, both heavenly and earthly. It is a title of God as commander of all powers. James 5:4 keeps the Hebrew form, "Lord Sabaoth".

25:6.t: "Mercy and steadfast love" (Hebrew rachamim; chasadim): the KJV's "tender mercies and lovingkindnesses". Rachamim, from rechem, "womb", means compassion, a mother's tender love (see Exodus 34:6); hasadim is the plural of hesed, loyal, committed love that keeps its promises (see Genesis 24:27).

25:10.t: "Steadfast love and faithfulness" (Hebrew hesed ve'emet): the KJV's "mercy and truth". hesed is loyal, committed love that keeps its promises, especially within a covenant; no single English word covers it, and the KJV uses "mercy", "kindness" and "lovingkindness"; emet means firmness, reliability, truth. The pair describes God's character. See Genesis 24:27 and Exodus 34:6.

27:4.t: "To gaze on the beauty of the LORD" (Hebrew lachazot beno'am YHWH): no'am means pleasantness, delight, kindness. The psalmist's single desire is to enjoy God's presence.

27:8.t: "Seek His face": to seek God's presence and favor. The Hebrew reads literally "To You my heart said, 'Seek My face'", the heart repeating God's own invitation.

27:14.t: "Wait for the LORD" (Hebrew qavveh el YHWH): qavah means to wait with eager expectation, like a stretched cord. It is the root of tiqvah, "hope" (Job 7:6).

29:3.t: "The voice of the LORD" (Hebrew qol YHWH): repeated seven times, like seven claps of thunder. A storm sweeps from the Mediterranean over Lebanon to the southern desert, and the psalm turns the thunder that Canaanites credited to Baal into praise of the LORD.

30:5.t: "Weeping may stay for the night, but joy comes in the morning": the verb lin, "lodge" or "spend the night", pictures weeping as an overnight guest who leaves at dawn.

31:5.t: "Into Your hands I commit my spirit" (Hebrew beyadkha aphqid ruchi): Jesus spoke these words as He died (Luke 23:46), adding "Father". Stephen echoed them (Acts 7:59). Ruach here means life itself.

31:15.t: "My times are in Your hands": every moment and season of life rests in God's care.

32:1.t: "Forgiven ... covered ... does not count against him" (Hebrew nesuy; kesuy; lo yachshov): three pictures of forgiveness: sin lifted away, sin covered over, and sin not credited to one's account (the same word as "counted" in Genesis 15:6). Paul quotes these verses in Romans 4:7-8 to show that God credits righteousness apart from works.

32:8.t: "I will instruct you": here God speaks. The pronoun "My eye" is capitalized accordingly.

33:6.t: "By the word of the LORD ... by the breath of His mouth" (Hebrew bidvar YHWH ... beruach piv): creation came by God's speech (Genesis 1:3) and His breath, ruach, which is also "spirit" (Genesis 1:2). John 1:1-3 builds on this: all things were made through the Word.

34:7.t: "The angel of the LORD": the heavenly messenger who acts for God and often speaks as God Himself (Genesis 16:7-13, Exodus 3:2). Lowercase pronouns are used, as in Genesis and Exodus.

34:8.t: "Taste and see that the LORD is good": 1 Peter 2:3 echoes this: "you have tasted that the Lord is good."

34:18.t: "Brokenhearted ... crushed in spirit": compare 51:17 and Isaiah 57:15. God draws near to those humbled by sorrow or by their sin.

34:20.t: "Not one of them will be broken": John 19:36 sees this fulfilled when Jesus' legs were not broken on the cross, together with the Passover rule (Exodus 12:46).

36:5.t: "Steadfast love ... faithfulness" (Hebrew hesed; emunah): hesed is loyal, committed love that keeps its promises, especially within a covenant; no single English word covers it, and the KJV uses "mercy", "kindness" and "lovingkindness" (see Genesis 24:27). Emunah, from the same root as amen, means firmness and reliability.

36:9.t: "In Your light we see light": God's presence is the source of all life and understanding. John 1:4 and 8:12 echo this: "In Him was life, and that life was the light of men."

37:4.t: "Take delight in the LORD" (Hebrew hit'annag): to find pleasure and joy in Him. The promise is not that God grants any wish, but that a heart delighting in Him will desire what He gives.

37:5.t: "Commit your way" (Hebrew gol, "roll"): roll your way onto the LORD, as one rolls a heavy burden onto another.

39:12.t: "A foreigner, a stranger" (Hebrew ger, toshav): Israel held the land as tenants of God, and the law calls them "foreigners and residents" before Him (see Leviticus 25:23). Hebrews 11:13 says the patriarchs confessed they were strangers on the earth.

40:7.t: "In the scroll" (Hebrew bimgillat sepher): the KJV's "in the volume of the book", the written law.

42:1.t: "As the deer pants ... my soul thirsts for God, for the living God": the soul (nephesh) also means throat; the image is of physical thirst. "The living God" (el chai) contrasts the true God with lifeless idols.

42:7.t: "Deep calls to deep": the roar of one torrent answers another, a picture of overwhelming trouble. The sea and waves are also signs of God's power over chaos, as when He struck down Rahab, the sea monster (see Job 26:12).

44:23.t: "Awake, Lord! Why do You sleep?": a bold lament. The psalmist knows God does not sleep (121:4), yet in suffering it feels as though He does.

45:6.t: "Your throne, O God": the psalm celebrates a royal wedding, and the king is addressed with titles that go beyond any human ruler. Hebrews 1:8-9 quotes these verses of the Son, who is both addressed as God and anointed by God. Because of this, the pronouns for the King are capitalized throughout the psalm, while those for the bride are not. Some modern Bibles read verse 6 as "Your divine throne" or "Your throne is God's throne".

46:1.t: "An ever-present help in trouble" (Hebrew ezrah betsarot nimtsa me'od): literally "a help in troubles, very much found". God is found to be a help at exactly the moment He is needed. Martin Luther's hymn "A Mighty Fortress" is based on this psalm.

46:10.t: "Be still" (Hebrew harpu): let go, stop striving, relax your grip. It is spoken first to the warring nations, then to God's people: stop fighting and acknowledge who is God.

47:5.t: "God has ascended" (Hebrew alah): the picture is of God going up to His throne after victory, perhaps reenacted by bringing the ark into the temple. Christian tradition reads this psalm on Ascension Day.

49:7.t: "No one can redeem ... But God will redeem me" (Hebrew padah): to buy back by paying a price (see Exodus 13:13). No amount of wealth can buy a life back from death, but God can and will. "He will surely take me" (yiqqacheni) uses the verb used of Enoch (Genesis 5:24) and Elijah (2 Kings 2:10), suggesting a hope beyond death.

49:15.t: "No one can redeem ... But God will redeem me" (Hebrew padah): to buy back by paying a price (see Exodus 13:13). No amount of wealth can buy a life back from death, but God can and will. "He will surely take me" (yiqqacheni) uses the verb used of Enoch (Genesis 5:24) and Elijah (2 Kings 2:10), suggesting a hope beyond death.

50:14.t: "Thank offerings" (Hebrew todah): the word means both thanks and confession, acknowledging what God has done; the thank offering was given after God answered prayer (see Leviticus 7:12). God wants grateful hearts, not the animals He already owns.

51:1.t: "Blot out ... wash ... cleanse": three pictures of forgiveness, matching three words for sin: pesha (rebellion), avon (iniquity, twistedness), chatta't (missing the mark); see Exodus 34:7.

51:4.t: "Against You, You only, have I sinned": though David wronged Bathsheba and Uriah, all sin is ultimately against God. Paul quotes the second half in Romans 3:4.

51:10.t: "Create in me a pure heart" (Hebrew bara): the verb used in Genesis 1:1, used only of God's creating. The psalmist asks for a new creation, not a repair.

51:11.t: "Your Holy Spirit" (Hebrew ruach qodshekha): one of only three Old Testament uses of the phrase (with Isaiah 63:10-11). David had seen the Spirit depart from Saul (1 Samuel 16:14).

51:17.t: "A broken and contrite heart" (Hebrew lev nishbar venidkeh): a heart shattered and crushed by awareness of sin. This is the sacrifice God accepts; compare 34:18 and Isaiah 57:15.

55:22.t: "Cast your cares on the LORD" (Hebrew hashlekh al YHWH yehavekha): yehav, "burden" or "what He has given you", appears only here. 1 Peter 5:7 echoes the verse: "Cast all your anxiety on Him because He cares for you."

56:4.t: "What can mere mortals do to me?" (Hebrew basar, "flesh"): human power is weak and temporary compared with God's. Hebrews 13:6 quotes the similar Psalm 118:6.

56:11.t: "What can mere mortals do to me?" (Hebrew basar, "flesh"): human power is weak and temporary compared with God's. Hebrews 13:6 quotes the similar Psalm 118:6.

57:3.t: "Steadfast love and faithfulness" (Hebrew hesed ve'emet): hesed is loyal, committed love that keeps its promises, especially within a covenant; no single English word covers it, and the KJV uses "mercy", "kindness" and "lovingkindness"; emet means firmness, reliability, truth (see Genesis 24:27). Here they are pictured as messengers God sends.

57:10.t: "Steadfast love and faithfulness" (Hebrew hesed ve'emet): hesed is loyal, committed love that keeps its promises, especially within a covenant; no single English word covers it, and the KJV uses "mercy", "kindness" and "lovingkindness"; emet means firmness, reliability, truth (see Genesis 24:27). Here they are pictured as messengers God sends.

61:7.t: "Steadfast love and faithfulness" (Hebrew hesed ve'emet): hesed is loyal, committed love that keeps its promises, especially within a covenant; no single English word covers it, and the KJV uses "mercy", "kindness" and "lovingkindness"; emet means firmness, reliability, truth (see Genesis 24:27). Here they are pictured as messengers God sends.

61:2.t: "The rock that is higher than I": a place of safety the psalmist cannot reach on his own; God must lead him there.

61:6.t: "The king ... enthroned in God's presence forever": first a prayer for David's line, which later readers took as pointing to the Messiah, the King who reigns forever.

62:11.t: "One thing God has spoken, two things I have heard": a Hebrew way of saying the truth was heard clearly and repeatedly. The two truths are God's power (62:11) and His steadfast love (62:12).

63:3.t: "Your steadfast love is better than life" (Hebrew tov chasdekha mechayyim): hesed, God's loyal, committed love that keeps its promises (see Genesis 24:27), is valued above life itself.

66:18.t: "If I had cherished sin in my heart": prayer offered while clinging to sin is not heard. The psalmist rejoices that this was not his case (66:19). Compare Isaiah 59:2.

68:5.t: "A father to the fatherless": God Himself takes the place of the missing father and husband. See Exodus 22:22-24, Deuteronomy 10:18.

68:18.t: "You ascended on high; You took many captives; You received gifts from people": the picture is of a victorious king going up to his throne with captives and tribute. Paul quotes this verse in Ephesians 4:8, following an interpretive reading, "gave gifts to men", and applies it to Christ's ascension and the gifts He gives the church.

69:4.t: "Those who hate me without reason": Jesus applies this to Himself in John 15:25.

69:9.t: "Zeal for Your house consumes me": the disciples remembered this verse when Jesus cleared the temple (John 2:17). Paul quotes the second line of Christ in Romans 15:3.

69:21.t: "Gall ... vinegar": the soldiers offered Jesus wine mixed with gall and then sour wine on the cross (Matthew 27:34, 27:48, John 19:28-30).

73:17.t: "Till I entered the sanctuary of God": the turning point of the psalm. In God's presence the psalmist sees the end of the wicked and the true good of nearness to God.

73:24.t: "Afterward You will take me into glory" (Hebrew achar kavod tiqqacheni): the verb laqach, "take", is used of Enoch and Elijah, whom God took to Himself (see 49:15). This is among the clearest Old Testament hopes of life with God after death.

73:26.t: "My portion": the psalmist's share and inheritance is God Himself, as He was for the Levites, who received no land; see 16:5.

74:14.t: "Leviathan": a great sea creature, perhaps the crocodile, and in poetry a symbol of chaos; see Job 41. Here it pictures the forces God defeated at the Red Sea and in creation.

75:8.t: "A cup ... of foaming wine": the cup of God's wrath, which the wicked must drink (Isaiah 51:17, Jeremiah 25:15, Revelation 14:10). Jesus prayed that "this cup" might pass from Him (Matthew 26:39).

78:38.t: "He was merciful" (Hebrew rachum): rachum comes from rechem, "womb", a mother's tender love (see Exodus 34:6). "He forgave" (yekhapper, "atoned for, covered"): to remove guilt so that the relationship with God is restored (see Exodus 29:33).

78:70.t: David the shepherd: God took him from caring for sheep to caring for His people. The picture of the king as shepherd prepares for the Good Shepherd (John 10:11).

80:3.t: "Restore us ... make Your face shine on us" (Hebrew hashivenu ... ha'er panekha): the refrain recalls the priestly blessing (Numbers 6:25) and grows each time: "O God", "God of hosts", "LORD God of hosts". Hashivenu, "turn us back", is from shuv, to turn around, the main Old Testament word for repentance and also for God restoring His people; see Deuteronomy 30:2.

80:7.t: "Restore us ... make Your face shine on us" (Hebrew hashivenu ... ha'er panekha): the refrain recalls the priestly blessing (Numbers 6:25) and grows each time: "O God", "God of hosts", "LORD God of hosts". Hashivenu, "turn us back", is from shuv, to turn around, the main Old Testament word for repentance and also for God restoring His people; see Deuteronomy 30:2.

80:19.t: "Restore us ... make Your face shine on us" (Hebrew hashivenu ... ha'er panekha): the refrain recalls the priestly blessing (Numbers 6:25) and grows each time: "O God", "God of hosts", "LORD God of hosts". Hashivenu, "turn us back", is from shuv, to turn around, the main Old Testament word for repentance and also for God restoring His people; see Deuteronomy 30:2.

80:8.t: The vine: Israel is pictured as a vine God brought from Egypt and planted (compare Isaiah 5:1-7). Jesus calls Himself "the true vine" (John 15:1).

80:17.t: "The man at Your right hand, the son of man": the king, or Israel itself, whom God raised up. Later readers heard a messianic hope here, echoed in Jesus' use of "Son of Man" (Daniel 7:13).

82:1.t: "Gods ... sons of the Most High" (Hebrew elohim; bene elyon): the psalm pictures God judging in His heavenly council. The "gods" may be human judges who rule in God's name (at Exodus 21:6 elohim may mean judges acting for God), or heavenly powers set over the nations (Deuteronomy 32:8 in the Greek). Jesus quotes verse 6 in John 10:34-36, arguing that if Scripture calls those who received God's word "gods", He is not blaspheming in calling Himself God's Son.

82:6.t: "Gods ... sons of the Most High" (Hebrew elohim; bene elyon): the psalm pictures God judging in His heavenly council. The "gods" may be human judges who rule in God's name (at Exodus 21:6 elohim may mean judges acting for God), or heavenly powers set over the nations (Deuteronomy 32:8 in the Greek). Jesus quotes verse 6 in John 10:34-36, arguing that if Scripture calls those who received God's word "gods", He is not blaspheming in calling Himself God's Son.

83:18.t: "Yahweh" (Hebrew YHWH): God's personal name, which the KJV usually prints LORD. This is one of the places where the KJV prints JEHOVAH, so the name is spelled out. See Exodus 6:3.

84:11.t: "A sun and shield": the only place in Scripture where God is called a sun, picturing Him as the source of life, light and protection.

85:10.t: "Steadfast love and faithfulness meet together; righteousness and peace kiss each other": four of God's attributes pictured as persons embracing. Hesed and emet: loyal covenant love and firm reliability (see Genesis 24:27); tsedeq and shalom: righteousness and wholeness. Christian writers have seen their meeting fulfilled at the cross.

86:11.t: "Give me an undivided heart" (Hebrew yached levavi): literally "unite my heart", make it single and whole in devotion. Compare the Shema, Deuteronomy 6:4-5.

86:15.t: "Compassionate and gracious ... slow to anger, abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness": a quotation of God's description of Himself in Exodus 34:6. "Compassionate" comes from the word for womb, a mother's tender love; "gracious" is kindness to the undeserving; "slow to anger" is literally "long of nostrils"; "steadfast love and faithfulness" are hesed and emet, loyal covenant love and firm reliability. See the note there.

89:3.t: The covenant with David: God's oath to establish David's line and throne forever (2 Samuel 7:12-16). The psalm sets this unbreakable promise against the collapse of the kingdom (89:38-51), and its question finds an answer in the Messiah, the Son of David (Luke 1:32-33, Acts 13:34).

89:28.t: The covenant with David: God's oath to establish David's line and throne forever (2 Samuel 7:12-16). The psalm sets this unbreakable promise against the collapse of the kingdom (89:38-51), and its question finds an answer in the Messiah, the Son of David (Luke 1:32-33, Acts 13:34).

89:27.t: "My firstborn": the firstborn held the place of highest honor. Colossians 1:15 and Revelation 1:5 use the word of Christ.

90:4.t: "A thousand years in Your sight are like a day": God stands outside time. 2 Peter 3:8 draws on this verse.

90:12.t: "Teach us to number our days, that we may gain a heart of wisdom": knowing life is short leads to wise living.

91:11.t: "He will command His angels concerning you": Satan quoted these verses to Jesus in the temptation, leaving out "to guard you in all your ways". Jesus answered with Deuteronomy 6:16 (Matthew 4:6-7). The promise is of protection in faithful obedience, not license to test God.

91:14.t: "Because he loves Me" (Hebrew ki vi chashaq): chashaq means to cling to in love, a word for strong attachment or desire; see Deuteronomy 7:7.

93:1.t: "The LORD reigns" (Hebrew YHWH malakh): the theme of Psalms 93-99, celebrating God as King over creation and all nations.

96:10.t: "The LORD reigns" (Hebrew YHWH malakh): the theme of Psalms 93-99, celebrating God as King over creation and all nations.

95:7.t: "Today, if only you would hear His voice": Hebrews 3:7-4:11 quotes these verses at length, warning against unbelief and holding out God's "rest" as still available to His people.

95:11.t: "My rest" (Hebrew menuchati): the rest of the promised land, which the wilderness generation forfeited. Hebrews 4 links it to God's Sabbath rest at creation and to the rest that remains for the people of God.

100:5.t: "His steadfast love endures forever" (Hebrew le'olam chasdo): a refrain found throughout the Psalms (106:1, 107:1, 118:1, and every verse of Psalm 136) and in Chronicles. hesed is loyal, committed love that keeps its promises, especially within a covenant; no single English word covers it, and the KJV uses "mercy", "kindness" and "lovingkindness". See Genesis 24:27.

102:25.t: "In the beginning You laid the foundations of the earth ... You remain the same": Hebrews 1:10-12 applies these words to the Son, through whom God made the world and who never changes (Hebrews 13:8).

103:3.t: "Who forgives ... heals ... redeems ... crowns ... satisfies": a list of God's benefits. "Redeems your life from the pit" (go'el): The go'el was the family member who bought back land, freed a kinsman from slavery, or avenged his blood; God acts as His people's next of kin. See Exodus 6:6.

103:8.t: "Compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in steadfast love": a quotation of God's description of Himself in Exodus 34:6. "Compassionate" comes from the word for womb, a mother's tender love; "gracious" is kindness to the undeserving; "slow to anger" is literally "long of nostrils", taking a long time for anger to flare; "steadfast love" is hesed, loyal covenant love. See the note there.

103:13.t: "As a father has compassion" (Hebrew rachem): the verb from rechem, "womb"; tender, parental love (see Exodus 34:6).

104:30.t: "When You send Your Spirit" (Hebrew ruach): ruach means spirit, wind and breath, linking verse 29 ("You take away their breath") with verse 30. God's Spirit is the source of all life; see Genesis 1:2 and 2:7.

106:23.t: "Stood in the breach" (Hebrew amad bapperets): like a soldier standing in a broken wall to hold back the enemy, Moses stood between God's wrath and the people. Ezekiel 22:30 uses the same picture.

106:31.t: "Credited to him as righteousness": the same phrase as Genesis 15:6, used of Phinehas's zeal (Numbers 25:7-13).

106:45.t: "Relented" (Hebrew nacham): the word means to be sorry, grieved or moved to change course, not an admission of a mistake. See Genesis 6:6 and Exodus 32:14.

107:2.t: "The redeemed of the LORD" (Hebrew ge'ule YHWH): those bought back by their divine kinsman. The go'el was the family member who bought back land, freed a kinsman from slavery, or avenged his blood; see Exodus 6:6. The psalm gives four pictures of rescue: wanderers, prisoners, the sick, and sailors in a storm, each ending with the same refrain of thanks for God's hesed.

110:1.t: "The LORD says to my Lord" (Hebrew ne'um YHWH ladoni): the first "LORD" is God's personal name; the second, adoni, means "my lord" or "my master". David speaks of a king greater than himself. Jesus asked how the Messiah could be David's son if David called him "Lord" (Matthew 22:41-46). This is the Old Testament verse most often quoted in the New Testament (Acts 2:34-35, Hebrews 1:13, 10:12-13). Following this reading, the pronouns for the Lord addressed are capitalized.

110:4.t: "A priest forever, in the order of Melchizedek": Melchizedek was both king of Salem and priest of God Most High (Genesis 14:18). Hebrews 5-7 shows that Jesus is this eternal king-priest, whose priesthood is greater than Aaron's.

111:10.t: "The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom": the fear of the LORD is reverent awe and trust that shows itself in turning from evil; see Job 28:28 and Proverbs 1:7. "Beginning" (reshit) means the first step and the foundation.

115:1.t: "Not to us, LORD, not to us": glory belongs to God alone, because of His hesed and emet, His loyal covenant love and His faithfulness; see Genesis 24:27.

116:13.t: "The cup of salvation": a cup of wine poured out in thanks to God, perhaps at the thank-offering meal. Christians have connected it with the cup of the Lord's Supper.

116:15.t: "Precious in the sight of the LORD is the death of His faithful servants": the death of the faithful is costly and significant to God; He does not treat it lightly. "Faithful servants" (chasidav) is related to hesed.

118:22.t: "The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone": the cornerstone (rosh pinnah, "head of the corner") holds the whole building together. Jesus applied this to Himself (Matthew 21:42), and Peter preached it (Acts 4:11, 1 Peter 2:7).

118:25.t: "LORD, save us!" (Hebrew hoshi'ah na): the source of "Hosanna", which the crowds shouted, with verse 26, as Jesus entered Jerusalem (Matthew 21:9). Originally a plea, it became a shout of praise.

118:26.t: "Blessed is He who comes in the name of the LORD": a blessing on the pilgrim or king entering the temple; the Gospels apply it to Jesus (Mark 11:9, Luke 13:35).

119:11.t: "I have hidden Your word in my heart": treasured it, stored it within as a guard against sin.

119:105.t: "Your word is a lamp for my feet": a small oil lamp lit the next step on a dark path; God's word gives light for daily living.

119:165.t: "Great peace" (Hebrew shalom rav): shalom means peace, wholeness, and well-being with God and others (see Leviticus 3:1). "Nothing can make them stumble" (mikhshol): no obstacle can trip them.

119:176.t: "I have strayed like a lost sheep": the psalm ends not with self-confidence but with a plea for the Shepherd to seek His servant. Compare Isaiah 53:6 and Luke 15:4-7.

121:4.t: "Will neither slumber nor sleep": unlike the gods of the nations, who were imagined to sleep (1 Kings 18:27), the LORD is always watchful.

121:5.t: "Watches over" (Hebrew shamar): used six times in this short psalm; the same verb as in the priestly blessing, "The LORD bless you and keep you" (Numbers 6:24).

121:7.t: "Watches over" (Hebrew shamar): used six times in this short psalm; the same verb as in the priestly blessing, "The LORD bless you and keep you" (Numbers 6:24).

127:2.t: "He grants sleep to those He loves": the Hebrew may also be read "He gives to His beloved while they sleep". Either way, anxious toil achieves nothing apart from God.

130:3.t: "If You kept a record of sins ... But with You there is forgiveness": this was a favorite psalm of Martin Luther. Forgiveness leads not to carelessness but to reverence ("that You may be revered").

130:7.t: "Steadfast love" (Hebrew hesed) and "full redemption" (peduth): hesed is God's loyal, committed love that keeps its promises (see Genesis 24:27); peduth, from padah, is redemption by paying a price (see Exodus 13:13).

132:17.t: "A horn grow for David" (Hebrew atsmiach qeren): "grow" (tsamach) is related to tsemach, "Branch", a title for the Messiah (Jeremiah 23:5, Zechariah 3:8). Zechariah echoes this verse in Luke 1:69.

139:7.t: "Your Spirit" (Hebrew ruach): ruach means spirit, wind and breath; here it is God's presence filling all places; see 104:30.

139:13.t: "Inmost being": the KJV's "reins", literally "kidneys" (kilyot), the seat of the deepest emotions. "Knit me together" (sakhakh) means to weave or cover.

139:16.t: "My unformed body" (Hebrew golem): an embryo, the only use of the word in the Bible. God saw and planned the psalmist's life before birth.

139:21.t: "Hate ... perfect hatred": complete rejection of those in open rebellion against God, taking God's side; verses 23-24 at once turn the searching light on the psalmist's own heart.

141:2.t: "Like incense ... like the evening sacrifice": prayer is offered as worship in place of the temple offerings. Compare Revelation 5:8 and 8:3-4.

143:10.t: "Your good Spirit": the Spirit of God, as at Nehemiah 9:20. "Level ground" (erets mishor): ground without obstacles.

145:8.t: "Gracious and compassionate, slow to anger and rich in steadfast love": a quotation of God's description of Himself in Exodus 34:6; see 103:8. "Gracious" is kindness to the undeserving; "compassionate" comes from the word for womb, a mother's tender love; "slow to anger" is literally "long of nostrils"; "steadfast love" is hesed, loyal covenant love.

149:6.t: "A double-edged sword in their hands": the psalm celebrates God's judgment on the nations carried out by His people in Israel's history. The New Testament speaks of the word of God as the sword of the Spirit (Ephesians 6:17, Hebrews 4:12).

150:6.t: "Everything that has breath" (Hebrew kol hanneshamah): neshamah is the breath God breathed into man (Genesis 2:7). The life God gives is returned to Him in praise.
